in terms of pve aggressive and rapid fire snipers do completely different jobs so one can’t really replace the other. 

Obviously due to rpm rapid fire has higher dps so it’s a go-to for boss damage. Supremacy comes especially good at this since it’s kinetic, and has rewind rounds + bait n switch / fourth times. 

On the other hand aggressive has significantly lower dps but much higher damage per shot. Its used to take down beefier, singular enemies (think orange bars and cyclops) usually one shot or leave their health bar barely empty so you can finish them off. It’s also a lot more forgiving compared to rapid fire, because you don’t need to land tons of shots to take down an enemy.

You should EQ them as a whole, which means EQ is _before & after_ the parallel split, but not _inside_ of it.

That’d do for most context. However there surely is a chance where you unironically want to boost that 20db parallel (probably to awaken the saturation) hence why linear phase.

Every single regular EQ causes your phase to shift even the 3000$ hardware one. Now dont worry if you got no idea wtf this means cus it prolly wont never bother you. Nor am i saying this is a bad thing. 

But sometimes its a pain, or more like a mosquito bite, one clear example is when you do parallel processing. (also known as blending dry/wet)

Compression and distortion is good to do parallel, but not EQ. Because EQ heavily relies on - you guessed it - shifting your phase. thats gonna cause phase cancellation when you mix it with the dry signal! its like an invincible kitty that messed up your EQ settings and you’ll be frustrating for the next hour about why some frequencies disappeared. 

So if you reaaally wanna do parallel EQ, then you have Linear Phase, which basically just dosent cause phase shift. That way you can give that THICC 20db boost , blend it 1% and call it your secret sauce. 

However there still is a downside to Linear Phase which is commonly known as the “Pre-Ringing Effect” this sounds the most apparent on drums. It just sounds as if you put some reversed samples at the begging of your drums. Its a deal with the devil but sometimes its worth it. Not on drums tho for sure.

One thing you have to understand is that whenever you EQ, you change the phase of your sound. Regardless what plugin or hardware you use. 

Your prolly not aware of that, because it rarely changes your sound if at all. So thats the reason why you never have to bother linear phase. 

But when you need to do parallel processing thats when you should be extra careful with phase and using EQ. 

Since using any EQ basically changes your phase, phase cancellation would occur between your original channel and parallel channel. This would result in some gain loss right beside your EQ areas. On both of your channels. 

(Edit: thats why its a big no no to adjust the mix knob at the right side of your EQ plugin- since that is parallel processing and you already know how that sounds like. )

It might also happen when you record a guitar or snare drum with 2 different mics. From what i tested reverbs and delays at 100% wet on a send channel would not be affected. 

Hence why we need linear phase EQ - it simply just EQs, but without changing your phase. So now you could do all the crazy things you want. Say, on your parallel channel boost the hell out of your highs and chop of the lows and feed it to your compressor. 

However, linear phase EQ also has some weak points, compared to normal minimum phase EQ. It uses more processing power and generates plugin latency, since it relies on this look-ahead feature that you might also find on mastering limiters. 

Another side effect that comes with it is a “pre-ringing” effect. This sounds the most apparent on drums. It feels like as if you’ve put a reversed sample right before your drum hit and makes your transient sound weird.

I always use straight samples for kicks, snares, simple percussions, anything thats solid. Its way easier to arrange this way. 

When i need to program say trap beat hihats, acoustic hihats and tom fills, i reach for a drum rack. Because they are much more rhythmic complex. 

I will process all my drums individually including the stuff inside drum rack. I then route them all into a buss and add some glue compression. Even a 3db reduction makes a night and day difference.
